sections.facts: The respondent, in the first of these appeals, was manufacturing different varieties of printing paper including wrapping paper falling under Item No. 17 of the erstwhile Central Excise Tariff. The appellant issued a show cause notice to the respondent for the alleged violation of Rules 9(1), 173 F and 173 G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 in respect of wrapping paper removed outside the factory without payment of Central Excise duty, and for imposition of penalty. The Superintendent (Technical) held against the respondent, and on appeal, the Collector (Appeals) rejected the claim. On further appeal, the Customs, Excise and Gold (Control) Appellate Tribunal referred to its own decision, which is the subject matter of the other appeals herein, and set aside the order of the Collector. The facts leading to the other appeals are similar, and the issue involved is the same. The Revenue filed the appeals before the Supreme Court under Section 35L of the Central Excises & Salt Act.
sections.statute: Item No. 17 of the erstwhile Central Excise Tariff; Rules 9(1), 173 F, and 173 G of the Central Excise Rules, 1944; Section 2(f) and Section 35L of the Central Excises & Salt Act; and Notification No. 18A/83 CE dated 9th July, 1983.
sections.argument: Showing cause, the respondent contended that the wrapping paper was captively consumed and utilised as a component part of other varieties of paper and as such no duty was payable, placing reliance on Section 2(f) of the Act and Notification No. 18A/83 CE dated 9th July, 1983. On behalf of the Revenue, it was contended that wrapping paper cannot be deemed to be a component part because it did not become an integral part of the packed paper. The assessee contended that wrapping paper was a raw material or component part of the wrapped paper, relying on Section 2(f) of the Act which includes any process incidental or ancillary to the completion of a manufactured product. It was also urged that Revenue had itself considered the stage of wrapped or packed paper as the stage at which goods should be entered in the statutory production register.
sections.analysis: 'Manufacture' in the sense it is used in excise law is not complete until and unless wrapping is done. Excise is a duty on manufacture, which is the process or activity bringing into existence new, identifiable, and distinct goods that are marketed or marketable in the market as such. Duty is levied on goods, and as the Act does not define 'goods', the word carries its ordinary dictionary meaning as something that can ordinarily come to the market to be bought and sold and is known to the market as such. The finished goods were cut to size and packed paper which, according to trade practice and Indian standards, consisted of wrapping paper and wrapped paper; the market was for paper packed and wrapped in paper. Therefore, anything entering into and forming part of that process must be deemed to be raw material or a component part of the end product used in its manufacture. Processes incidental or ancillary to wrapping are included in manufacture, and manufacture is not complete until wrapped. Where any process is so integrally connected with ultimate production that, but for it, manufacture or processing would be commercially inexpedient, articles required in that process fall within 'in the manufacture of goods'. To be marketable, it was an essential requirement for goods to be wrapped in paper; anything required to make goods marketable forms part of manufacture, and materials used for the same constitute component parts for the end product.
